title: IB & Analysis, Lesson 5: A combined case - valuing one company by several methods
subtitle: DCF, comps and precedent transactions give three different numbers - so which do you believe?
openingQuestion: Valuing the same company gives 100,000d per share by DCF, 85,000d by comps and 110,000d by precedent transactions. What is the right way to present the conclusion?
openingOptions: Take only the highest figure, to persuade the client
Present a valuation range built from all three methods
Use only the DCF because it is the most scientific method, and set the other two aside entirely
Take a simple average of the three figures without offering any further explanation at all
explanation: Standard industry practice is to present a valuation RANGE combining several methods, usually illustrated with a football field chart - each method produces a range on its own assumptions, and the overlap between them is generally treated as the most reliable zone. No method is absolutely right; each has its own strengths and limits.

diagram.label: DCF - built on assumptions about future cash flow
Comps - built on how the market prices peers today
Precedent transactions - built on M&A prices actually paid
Combined into a valuation range (the football field)

realWorldExample.description: In real IPO and M&A processes, investment banks always present a football field chart - a set of horizontal bars showing the range each method produces (DCF, comps, precedent transactions, the 52-week trading range and so on) so that the board and investors see the whole picture, rather than placing absolute trust in a single number.

quiz.question: Why is a DCF result far more sensitive than comps to a small change in one assumption (say long-run growth rising by 0.5%)?
options: Because DCF uses more input variables than the comps method
Because terminal value is 60-80% of the model's total value
Because DCF requires forecasting the full five years of statements
Because comps are always based on audited historical figures
quiz.explanation: Terminal value (representing the cash flows beyond the detailed forecast period) is usually most of a DCF's value - a small change in the long-run growth assumption or in WACC is multiplied through the Gordon growth formula (dividing by WACC minus g), which makes the final answer very sensitive to them. This is why a DCF always needs a sensitivity analysis alongside it.

quiz.question: When the three methods produce results very far apart (say 50,000d versus 150,000d), what does that usually say about the company being valued?
options: Pick the middle result immediately, to be on the safe side
There is certainly a calculation error in at least one of the three
The company is changing model, so the readings diverge
Take the simple average of the three as the final conclusion
quiz.explanation: A wide spread between valuation methods is usually not a calculation error but a genuine signal - it shows a high level of uncertainty (the market disagrees about prospects, good comparable data is missing, or the business is mid-transition). The width of the range is itself useful information, not just its midpoint.

quiz.question: Three valuation methods produce three very different numbers. What is the right way to read that?
options: The further apart the results, the more reliable the model is
The two furthest results must be removed from the table
Trust only the method landing nearest the market price
They answer three different questions, so divergence is normal
quiz.explanation: Each method measures something different: intrinsic value on your assumptions, what the market is paying, and what a strategic buyer once paid. The difference between them is itself the information.

quiz.question: Why is terminal value in a discounted cash flow model so sensitive?
options: Because the denominator is the gap between two close numbers
Because it sits at the end of the model and accumulates every error
Because it is computed as a multiple of the final forecast year
Because it is not discounted back to today like the other years
quiz.explanation: When the denominator is only about 7-9%, moving it by 2 percentage points changes the answer by tens of percent. That is why the sensitivity table is a required part of the work rather than an optional extra.

quiz.question: Why is a valuation range chart more useful than a single target number when presenting to management?
options: Because it always gives a wide range and is therefore hard to prove wrong
Because it shows how the conclusion depends on method and assumptions
Because industry standards require every valuation report to be presented as a range
Because a range removes the error inherent in each individual method
quiz.explanation: A single number hides all of the uncertainty behind it. A range forces the discussion to where it belongs: which assumption is pulling the result, and how far you believe that assumption.

keyTakeaways: Present a valuation range combining several methods (a football field chart) rather than committing to one absolute figure
DCF is highly sensitive to long-run assumptions (growth, WACC) because terminal value is most of the value
A wide spread between methods signals high uncertainty; it is not merely a calculation error

practicePrompt.question: DCF values the company at 8,000 billion, comps at 9,500 billion and precedent transactions at 10,500 billion. How should the analyst present the final result to management?
options: Present a combined valuation range rather than committing to one absolute figure
Take only the highest figure (10,500 billion), for the advantage it gives in a sale negotiation
Take only the DCF figure, since that is always the most accurate method in every situation
Take a simple average of the three figures without explaining the divergence between them
practicePrompt.explanation: Present a valuation range combining several methods rather than committing to one absolute figure. Each method has its own strengths and weaknesses, and presenting a range (the football field) is standard practice in professional valuation.

application.title: Build a football field for a stock you follow
application.message: Value the same business by DCF, comps and precedents, then plot the three ranges on one axis. Where the three overlap is the reliable zone; where they come apart is what you need to be able to explain before drawing any conclusion.
application.secondary: Run a two-way DCF sensitivity on WACC and long-run growth. If the resulting range is twice the market price wide, what you have learned is that the model has not decided anything yet.

sections.text: DCF, comps and precedent transactions give three different numbers for the same company - so which do you believe?
The football field: present a range, not a point

Standard industry practice is to present a valuation RANGE combining several methods rather than committing to a single number. DCF is highly sensitive to long-run assumptions, because terminal value is usually 60-80% of a DCF's value - a small change in long-run growth or WACC is multiplied through the Gordon growth formula. A wide spread between methods is usually not a calculation error but a signal of how genuinely uncertain the company is.

sections.title: The three methods answer three different questions
sections.subtitle: Their divergence is normal, because they are not asking the same thing

concepts.def: What is the business worth on your own assumptions about the future? Independent of market sentiment, but very sensitive to the long-run assumptions.

concepts.vi: So sánh công ty tương đương
concepts.def: What is the market paying for similar businesses right now? It reflects real transactions, but reproduces the market's mispricing as well.
What has a buyer of a whole business actually paid? Usually sets the upper bound of the range, because it includes control and synergies.

sections.title: Why terminal value dominates a discounted cash flow result
sections.equation: Terminal value = final-year FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g)

example.title: How sensitive the denominator is
example.calculation: r = 12%, g = 3% → denominator 9% · r = 11%, g = 4% → denominator 7%
example.result: Terminal value rises about 29% from a 1 percentage point change in each variable
example.explanation: Because the denominator is the difference between two close numbers, every small change is amplified sharply. This is why a DCF result must always come with a sensitivity table and should never be presented as a single figure.

items: A narrow range: the methods agree, so confidence is higher. Still check whether that is because they share one optimistic set of assumptions.

A wide range: the business is hard to value - uncertain growth, a business model in transition, or dependence on a few things nobody can forecast. A wide range is an honest answer, not a sign of sloppy work.
One method far from the other two: a signal to investigate, not to discard. It usually points to an assumption differing markedly from what the market believes.

sections.label: The most important thing to present
sections.text: Not the final number, but the list of assumptions producing it and how the result moves as each one shifts. A valuation that lets the reader substitute their own assumptions and recompute is far more useful than a figure precise to the last dong that nobody can check.

lines: A wide valuation range is not a sign of poor analysis.
Sometimes it is the most honest answer available about a company that is hard to value.

summary.keyIdea: Present a valuation range combining several methods (a football field chart) rather than committing to one absolute figure
summary.commonMistake: Easy to miss: DCF is highly sensitive to long-run assumptions (growth, WACC) because terminal value is most of the value
summary.action: A wide spread between valuation methods signals high uncertainty; it is not merely a calculation error
